Name: corrective_check_foresight
Title: Worth Checking? A Prospective Internal Signal That Distinguishes Corrective from Confirmatory Self-Verification
Short Hypothesis: At the onset of a self-verification (recheck) step, the reasoning model's residual stream already linearly encodes whether an actual latent error exists to be caught, i.e., whether the impending check will be corrective (fixes the answer) or merely confirmatory (wastes tokens). This 'value-of-verification' signal is available before the check runs, is distinct from a plain answer-correctness or uncertainty signal, and gating verification on it lets us suppress confirmatory checks while preserving rare corrective ones, cutting tokens with no accuracy loss.
Related Work: A large recent cluster addresses redundant self-verification: probes that read whether the current answer is correct and early-exit (Reasoning Models Know When They're Right 2025; Temporal Predictors 2025; Gnosis 2025); reflection-direction steering tied to uncertainty (ReflCtrl 2025); wholesale suppression of self-affirmation/confirmatory rechecks (Efficient Reasoning via Suppression of Self-Affirmation 2025; Self-Verification Dilemma 2026 via offline experience retrieval); semantic-convergence early exit (PUMA 2026); and RL-based step-potential termination (SPAE 2026, ASRR 2025, Structured Reasoning 2026). All of these read either (a) whether the current answer is already correct/confident, or (b) whether reasoning has converged/is redundant, and then stop or suppress checks. Crucially, they conflate 'the answer is currently right' with 'this check is not worth doing.' But the rare corrective checks are exactly the ones that occur when the answer is currently WRONG - and blunt suppression kills them, causing accuracy loss on hard items. Our contribution is a different, prospective quantity: whether a latent error actually exists to be caught by the impending check (value-of-verification), read at check onset before the check is generated. This is not an answer-correctness probe applied reactively; it is a forward-looking predictor of a check's counterfactual utility, aimed precisely at preserving genuine self-correction that all suppression methods endanger. To our knowledge no prior work predicts a check's corrective-vs-confirmatory outcome from pre-check internal state.
Abstract: Reasoning models spend a large fraction of tokens on self-verification, yet analyses show the overwhelming majority of these rechecks are confirmatory - they re-confirm an already-correct result and change nothing - while a rare, precious few are corrective, catching a genuine error and fixing the answer. Existing efficiency methods suppress verification wholesale or exit when the current answer looks correct, but this endangers exactly the corrective checks that occur when the answer is wrong, risking accuracy loss on hard problems. We ask a sharper question: does the model already know, at the moment it begins a verification step, whether there is an actual error to be caught - that is, whether this check will be corrective or merely confirmatory - before performing it? We hypothesize the residual stream at check onset linearly encodes this value-of-verification signal, distinct from a plain answer-correctness or uncertainty signal. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we label each recheck as corrective or confirmatory by comparing the pre-check and post-check answers, train a lightweight probe on pre-check activations to predict the outcome, and test separability from a correctness probe. We causally validate by steering the signal and by gating: skip predicted-confirmatory checks, allow predicted-corrective ones. We compare token savings at fixed accuracy - and, critically, corrective-check recall and hard-item accuracy - against correctness-based early-exit, reflection steering, and wholesale confirmatory suppression. Our work reframes efficient verification as predicting a check's utility and offers a correction-preserving efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Rechecks are detectable and overwhelmingly confirmatory): Establishes the labels and the stakes the rest depends on. Data: GSM8K (1000-problem sample of 1319 test), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198); all restricted to extractable numeric/multiple-choice answers so an answer change is unambiguous. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Method: segment each trace into steps, detect recheck onsets via lexical cues ('let me check / verify / wait / recompute') plus a reflection-direction classifier; for each recheck read the model's implicit answer just before and just after the check (logit-lens / answer probe and the emitted intermediate answer), labeling CORRECTIVE if the answer changed (especially wrong->right) and CONFIRMATORY otherwise. Decisive metric: the corrective:confirmatory ratio per dataset/model, plus a human spot-check of 200 labeled rechecks for label accuracy. Convincing result: corrective checks are < 20% of all rechecks (confirming they are rare and that blunt suppression has real stakes) and human-validated label accuracy >= 90%. Indecision band: label accuracy in [80%, 90%) means the labels are usable but noisy — report probe results with this noise floor; below 80% the labeling is unreliable and downstream probes are uninterpretable, requiring a cleaner answer-extraction rule first. Negative result (corrective checks are common, e.g., > 40%) would remove the efficiency motivation, since most checks would be worth keeping.

Experiment 2 (H2 — A prospective value-of-verification signal is decodable at check onset, distinct from answer-correctness): The core test. Data: ~5000 labeled rechecks from Experiment 1 for probe fitting and 1500 held-out (from disjoint problems), with class weighting for the corrective minority. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B for robustness, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at each recheck onset extract residual-stream activations BEFORE any check content is generated, and fit per-layer linear probes to predict corrective vs confirmatory. Systems compared: the value-of-verification probe vs (a) a plain answer-correctness probe read at the same position, (b) an uncertainty / reflection-direction score, (c) a prior-text bag-of-words classifier. Decisive metric: corrective-vs-confirmatory AUROC on held-out problems, reported with precision-recall on the corrective class given imbalance. Secondary: partial correlation and principal angle between the value-of-verification direction and the correctness direction. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 at some layer, a corrective-class precision-recall clearly above the base-rate line, a partial correlation with the corrective label >= 0.25 after removing the correctness probe, and principal angle >= 30 degrees from the correctness direction. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the signal is real but largely reducible to correctness — reported as an entangled utility correlate; AUROC < 0.65 or partial correlation < 0.10 means 'check utility' reduces to answer-correctness and H2 fails. Negative result would collapse the contribution into existing correctness-probe methods.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal validation: steering the signal shifts realized check outcomes): Tests that the direction causally governs whether a check corrects. Data: 400 held-out rechecks. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is adding/subtracting the value-of-verification direction at check onset, dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: value-of-verification steering vs matched random-direction and correctness-direction controls. Decisive metric: the change in realized corrective rate (fraction of checks that actually change the answer) as a function of steering dose. Convincing result: a monotone dose-response in which positive steering raises and negative steering lowers the realized corrective rate by >= 10 percentage points, exceeding both controls by >= 8 points, plus activation-patching localization to a small set of layers. Indecision band: an effect in [4, 10) points or not separable from the random control by > 5 points is weak causal evidence, reported as such. Negative result (no outcome shift) would mean the decodable signal is not causally operative, weakening but not killing the gating application, which only needs prediction.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Correction-preserving gating cuts tokens at fixed accuracy while keeping corrective checks): The applied test of the efficiency claim. Data: full GSM8K sample, MATH500, AIME, GPQA held-out from probe fitting. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; training-free gate = at each recheck onset read the probe and skip the check when the predicted-confirmatory score is below threshold tau, else allow it; 3 seeds. Systems compared: no intervention, correctness-based early-exit, reflection steering, wholesale self-affirmation suppression, PUMA-style convergence exit, and our gate. Decisive metric: corrective-check recall (fraction of genuinely corrective checks allowed to run) at matched token savings, read jointly with hard-strata accuracy (AIME and the hardest MATH/GPQA tercile). Secondary: overall accuracy, mean tokens, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy. Convincing result: at token savings matching wholesale suppression (within 3% of its mean-token reduction), our gate retains corrective-check recall >= 0.80 and hard-strata accuracy within +/- 1.0 point of no-intervention, whereas wholesale suppression loses > 3 points on hard strata. Indecision band: corrective recall in [0.60, 0.80) at matched savings, or hard-strata accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points, means the gate helps but does not cleanly beat suppression — reported as a modest improvement; recall < 0.60 or accuracy drop > 3 points means the gate fails its correction-preserving promise. Negative result (no better recall/accuracy than suppression at equal savings) would refute the practical claim while leaving the mechanistic H2 finding.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Threshold frontier, failure analysis, and generalization): Characterizes the trade-off and transfer. Data: the four datasets; failure cases mined from Experiment 4. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen. Method: sweep tau to trace the token-savings vs corrective-recall frontier; audit cases where the gate wrongly suppressed a corrective check (resulting accuracy loss) and wrongly allowed a confirmatory one (residual waste); transfer the probe and gate fit on one dataset/model to the others without retraining. Decisive metric: the tokens-vs-corrective-recall Pareto frontier and the retained gate performance on transfer targets. Convincing result: a frontier dominating the suppression baselines (higher corrective recall at equal tokens across a range of tau), and >= two-thirds of in-domain corrective recall retained on transfer. Indecision band: transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent transfer; below one-third means the probe is dataset/model-specific. Negative result would confine the method to its fitting conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The value-of-verification signal may be inseparable from a plain correctness signal (a corrective check is, almost by definition, one done when the answer is wrong); the separability, partial-correlation, and causal-steering analyses directly test this, and a null result would itself be an informative finding that 'check utility' reduces to answer-correctness. Labeling corrective vs confirmatory relies on detecting answer changes across a check, which is noisy for open-ended answers, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice with extractable answers and validate labels with human spot-checks. Corrective checks are rare, creating class imbalance that can inflate AUROC apparent performance; we report precision/recall and calibrated thresholds. Recheck-onset detection may be imperfect and miss implicit verification. Gating could still suppress a corrective check on a hard item (accuracy loss); the corrective-recall metric and hard-strata accuracy quantify this trade-off explicitly. Gains may not exceed strong suppression baselines on tokens alone - but the contribution is preserving accuracy/corrective recall at equal savings. Results may be model-family and scale specific.
